cards.memory: Data + Compute + Learning = the rise of computer vision.
cards.trap: Classification says WHAT is present, not WHERE.
explain: A computer sees an image as a grid of numbers: brightness 0–255 for grayscale, or three grids (red, green, blue) for colour. In PyTorch a batch of images has shape [batch, channels, height, width].
Different tasks ask different questions: classification (what is in the image?), detection (what, and where, as boxes?), segmentation (what is each pixel?).

tex.t: \text{image tensor} \in \mathbb R^{C \times H \times W}, \quad \text{grayscale } C = 1,\; \text{RGB } C = 3

cards.title: Why convolution (not dense layers)?
cards.hook: Dense layers forget which pixels were neighbours and need millions of weights.
cards.visual:
Problem with FCConvolution's answer
Flattening destroys 2D neighbourhoodslocal connectivity (3×3 patches)
224×224×3 = 150,528 inputs × 1,000 units = 150,528,000 weightsshared weights: one small filter reused everywhere
Hand-written rules can't cover every variationlearn the features from data
example: Two different '7's share a top bar, a descending diagonal and a lower stroke: local filters can match both.
cards.trap: Hand-engineered features must anticipate viewpoint, illumination, scale, deformation, occlusion, pose, clutter and intra-class variation.
explain: Hand-written rules ('ears at an angle < 35°') break under new viewpoints, lighting, sizes or occlusion.

A fully connected layer flattens the image into a long list, forgetting which pixels were neighbours, and needs a weight for every pixel-unit pair: 224×224×3 inputs × 1,000 units = 150 million weights.
Convolution fixes both: each unit looks only at a small patch (locality), the same small filter is reused everywhere (weight sharing), and stacked layers build edges → parts → objects (hierarchy).

cards.hook: Slide the filter, multiply element-wise, sum: one number per position.
example: Step 1: window rows 0-2, cols 0-2. Matches with +1 weights: 1; with −1 weights: 3 → 1 − 3 = −2.
cards.trap: Floor before +1, and padding counts twice (2P).
explain: A filter (kernel) is a small grid of weights, e.g. 3×3. Place it on the top-left patch of the image, multiply matching numbers, and add them up: that's one output value. Slide it one step (the stride) and repeat.
A big positive output means the patch looks like the filter's pattern (e.g. a diagonal stroke); negative means the opposite.
Padding adds a border of zeros so the filter can sit on the edges; it keeps the output larger.

cards.title: Filters, channels and parameter counts
cards.src: Lecture 7, slide 40; Key points about convolution filters and parameter counts
cards.hook: Each filter looks through ALL input channels and produces ONE output channel.
example: Two 3×3 filters on RGB with bias: (3×3×3 + 1)×2 = 56.
cards.memory: Filter depth = input depth; output depth = filter count.
cards.trap: Forgetting the bias, or forgetting × C_in.
explain: A filter is as deep as its input: on an RGB image a 3×3 filter is really 3×3×3 = 27 weights.
Each filter produces one output feature map, so the number of filters = the number of output channels.
Parameters = (weights per filter + 1 bias) × number of filters. The image size doesn't matter because the same filter is reused at every position.

cards.title: ReLU and pooling
cards.hook: ReLU keeps positive evidence; pooling keeps the strongest response and shrinks the map.

cards.memory: Pooling: keep the loudest voice in each room.
cards.trap: Pooling has NO learnable weights and does not change the number of channels.
explain: ReLU sets negative responses to 0, keeping only positive evidence and adding non-linearity.
Max pooling slides a window (usually 2×2, stride 2) and keeps only the largest value, halving the height and width. It has no weights to learn and keeps the number of channels.

cards.title: CNN classifiers, training & classic architectures
cards.hook: Conv + ReLU + pool blocks extract features; a head turns them into class scores.
formula: load pretrained → replace head → small LR → unfreeze selected → evaluate
example: AlexNet 2012 (large kernels, ReLU, dropout, GPU), VGG11 2014 (repeated 3×3), ResNet18 2015 (skip connections).
cards.memory: Spatial size shrinks, channels grow, receptive field grows.
cards.trap: Don't put softmax in the model when training with CrossEntropyLoss: it expects raw logits.
explain: A CNN classifier stacks blocks of conv → ReLU → pool (spatial size shrinks, channels grow), then flattens and uses a fully connected head to output class scores (logits).
Training repeats 5 steps per batch: zero the gradients, forward pass, compute the loss, backward pass, optimiser step.
ResNet adds skip connections: each block learns a correction F(x) and adds back x, so very deep networks still train.
